utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, would you like to continue, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Can you please bring Mr. Mujadzic in? Just before we start, it is my understanding that there is some confusion on the order of the next few witnesses and I would like to straighten that out so that all parties are clear. On the prior notice we had, we indicated that Mr. Doko would be proceeding next. However, because of the backlog and some of the delay that we had in the proceedings, it was required for us to send him back to Bosnia so he could participate in the elections that were scheduled in Mostar; it was required for him to be there. So he is not, in fact, in the country at this moment. We are bringing him back now. So, as currently planned, the next witness would be the witness P who was No. 12 on the original list, to be followed by witness No. 15, Selak, because, as we had indicated, the witness 14 or 10 was gone and that is why we had moved Mr. Doko up originally.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What about 13? Witness P is 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Right. Witness 13, because of his commitments, will follow -- the schedule was going to be P, Selak, Kranj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What number is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: 15 is Selak, Kranj is 17, then Doko 16 because of the time to bring him back here and then Mr. Vulliamy who is No. 13.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we have 12, 15, 17, 16 and 13, that is the current order?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is witness 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The first three in this new order are here and will be ready to go.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of course, witness P we will hear in closed session pursuant to the motion of the Prosecutor, unopposed, I believe, by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Would you continue, if there is nothing else preliminary?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. DR. MIRSAD MUJADZIC, recalled Examined by MR. KEEGAN, continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, when we left yesterday afternoon you had described a series, listed a series, of events or meetings which occurred in the first part of 1992, that you indicated caused some great concern to you for what was about to occur. We began with at least the first of those issues which was the meeting with Stojan Zupljanin, the head of the Security Services in Banja Luka. You indicated that one of the next significant issues was the proclamation of the Serb Republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the consequent proclamation of a Serb Assembly in opstina Prijedor. Can you describe the significance of those events, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Following the proclamation of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- I think this was at the beginning of 1992, I do not know the exact date -- came the proclamation of the Serb municipality of Prijedor which was published in the media. Milomir Stakic, who had legally performed the duty of Vice President of the Municipal Assembly, was proclaimed in the proclamation of the Serb municipality the President of the Serb municipality of Prijedor, and it was also announced that the Serb municipality of Prijedor would be joined to the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and I know for sure that the names of members of the municipal government were also published, the municipal government of the Serb municipality of Prijedor. I am afraid I do not remember all those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After the initial announcement of the establishment of this Serb municipality of Prijedor, did Dr. Stakic and the others still continue to perform their functions within the legitimate Municipal Assembly, the elected Municipal Assembly, of Prijedor for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic himself for a time did continue to come to work after the proclamation performing the duties of Vice President of the legitimate Municipal Assembly, as well as the elected members of the legitimate municipal government. Then perhaps just before the outbreak of the war, Milomir Stakic ceased coming to work in the building of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned as one of the significant events the takeover of the television transmitter which broadcast the signals to the Prijedor area. What was the significance of that takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a transmitter for the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on Mount Kozara at the point Lisina, just overlooking the city of Prijedor, and its function was to transmit the TV signal for the territory of the entire Sana River valley, therefore, the municipality of Prijedor and several other surrounding municipalities. At first, only the second TV channel was changed on this transmitter; whereas the first channel continued to transmit the first programme of the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The second channel transmitted the programme of television Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How would you describe the type of programming that was being received from the Belgrade channel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier on that Belgrade television had anyway been fully in the service of Milosevic's greater Serbia and propaganda, and this second channel continued to publicise Milosevic's propaganda on the idea of a greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At some point was the only channel of Bosnia-Herzegovina television also cut off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a certain time the first channel continued to function and then, I do not know the exact date, but maybe about a month later after the transmitter was taken over, was the channel of Bosnia-Herzegovina television cut off, so that the first channel, also first and second channel, transmitted only the programmes of television Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The next on your list of significant events was the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina particularly in the areas of Bijeljina and Brcko. What significance did those events have on the population in the opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People saw horrific pictures from Bijeljina where criminals and extremists belonging to paramilitary formations under the leadership of Arkan, under the command of Arkan, had killed tens and hundreds of non-Serb inhabitants in Bijeljina, and immediately afterwards Biljana Plavsic, who went on a visit to Bijeljina, shook hands, kissed and congratulated Arkan. That was a horrifying picture which shocked and frightened the non-Serb population in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At the time that Biljana Plavsic went to Bijeljina, congratulated Arkan, what was her position? What position did she hold in the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to then she held the position of member of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I think by then she was at the same time or maybe only a member or maybe Vice President of the newly proclaimed Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The next series of events you mentioned were the return of forces from the Croatian war and their redeployment in the Prijedor opstina. If I could have Exhibit 136 returned to the witness, please, and placed on the elmo? While we are waiting for that to be displayed on the elmo, Dr. Mujadzic, if you could briefly explain what forces were being returned from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After a cease-fire was established in Croatia, from the Croatian battle front at Lipik and Pakrac, two brigades returned to the region of Prijedor. They were the 5th Kozara Brigade, commanded by Colonel Pero Colic, and the 43rd Brigade where the commander was Colonel Arsic and his deputy was Major Radmilo Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of heavy weaponry did those brigades have with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had all heavy weaponry including tanks, cannon, guns and a large number of mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you point out using the opstina map there, Exhibit 136, where those forces and weapons were deployed in the opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, a part of the heavy weaponry was deployed in the region of Crna Dolina, or Black Valley, and Velika Palaciste, a part in the region of Lamovita, and a considerable portion of tanks and other heavy weaponry in the region of Omarska. In the region of the village of Miljakovci on Topica Brdo, Topica Hill, there were a number of mortars, and some smaller forces were deployed, I think, here in Niska Glava, I am not sure whether there was any heavy weaponry in Niska Glava.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After the return of these forces from the Croatian fronts, you indicated that the next significant events were a series of meetings with Colonel Arsic and his deputy, Radmilo Zeljaja. Can you explain what the nature of these meetings were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, the translation was that the meeting was with Zeljaja and Karadzic, was that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, Arsic and Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several such meetings. Some meetings started before the return of these brigades and they were meetings held through the Municipal Council for National Defence, and some meetings occurred after the return of these brigades. So if you could specify whether you want me to speak about the meetings before the arrival of these brigades or the meetings after the arrival of these brigades?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Let us start first with, obviously, the meetings before the return of the Brigade. Who called or asked for that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In formal, legal terms, the meeting was convened by the President of the Municipal Council for National Defence, who ex-officio was the President of the municipality, Muhamed Cehajic. However, he called the meeting upon the insistence of Colonel Arsic, and Arsic also asked that this meeting, which is normally attended in addition to the President of the municipality by function of their duties, the Prime Minister, the Chief of Police, the Commander of the communal headquarters of Territorial Defence units, the Municipal Secretary for National Defence, and the Vice President of the Executive Board who was also Commander of the headquarters of Civil Defence. Therefore, in addition to these regular members of the council, also invited to this meeting was I myself, as the President of the SDA, Simo Miskovic in his capacity of President of SDS, the President of HDZ, and I think also the President of the Social Democratic Party. He attended the first or the second meeting. Later on he was not invited. The main speaker at the meeting were Arsic and Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If could I have this next exhibit, Exhibit 140, handed to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When was this meeting, Dr. Mujadzic -- a date, as best as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact dates of those meetings. What I am sure of is that this was quite a bit before the return of these brigades. I think it was about a month or maybe more before the return of these brigades from the war front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If that photograph could be displayed on the elmo; the resolution was not very good on the computer. (To the witness): Dr. Mujadzic, do you recognise the man in the middle in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The photograph is not very clear. This is Colonel Arsic, Colonel Arsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender Exhibit 140.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 140?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 140 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask a question? What uniform is the first of those people in that photograph wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what kind of uniform. This is the first time I see this sign, this insignia. This was probably a photograph taken at a later stage after the time of our meetings. At that time Mico Kovacevic wore civilian clothes and the person you are asking about is Mico Kovacevic, President of the Executive Council of the Prijedor municipality, in other words, the President of the government of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I might be of some assistance, your Honour, this photograph is a still taken off a video which will be introduced later. You will see he is actually just wearing a T-shirt which, in fact, says "US Marines" on it which he has sewn a patch on, so it is not a uniform at all. (To the witness): This meeting, which you are about to describe, did take place before the takeover on 30th April 1992? The meeting which we are talking about that you were about to describe did take place before 30th April 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have understood the question, but I do not have a translation into Bosnian. I am sorry. No, it is all right. I can hear you now. I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To answer Judge McDonald's question, if I may repeat, in any event this meeting that you are about to describe did take place before 30th April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly much before April 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this meeting which Colonel Arsic asked for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time both brigades, Serb brigades, were on the front in Croatia. In the neighbouring municipality of Bosanska Dubica an incident occurred. Several Croatian soldiers, members of the National Guards known as "Zenga", apparently charged into some Serb villages and provoked certain incidents. After that, the surrounding Serb villages and the Serb population in Prijedor insisted that some form of protection be provided for them. At this meeting, Arsic proposed the mobilization of Territorial Defence of Prijedor, and that the most important buildings be protected in the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Concurrent with this mobilization was there a recommendation for the distribution of arms for the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after a number of these meetings, finally Arsic agreed that the weapons of Territorial Defence which were stored in the warehouses of the Yugoslav People's Army be distributed among the local communities, neighbourhood communities, and that a part of the municipal detachment of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Prijedor be mobilized. In each neighbourhood community 23 pieces were to be distributed, and I think for this detachment of the Prijedor municipality about 200 people were to be mobilized -- I am not quite sure of the figure -- for the city, for the town of Prijedor itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This decision or agreement for 23 pieces of arms to be distributed to each Mjesna Zajednica, was that based on the negotiations between the authorities of the legitimate government of the opstina and the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not exactly call them "negotiations"; it was more like Arsic's decision. We tried to ask for a larger number of weapons and, in addition to ordinary rifles, that other weapons be distributed as is normal for the mobilization of Territorial Defence, such as mortars and light guns, but he did not allow it, so that the weapons were limited to the 23 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you observe that some of the predominantly Muslim local communes were, in fact, distributed some of these weapons in accordance with this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not able to check that physically to see whether all these weapons were issued. What I am sure about is that in several local communes there were some complaints that some of these weapons were not in working order, that the number of pieces to be issued did not correspond to the number allowed, and in some local communes where there were Serbs and Muslims such as, for instance, Orlovci, the Muslims were not issued the weapons due them. They were only issued to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you observe in some of the Mjesna Zajednicas that were predominantly Muslim that, in fact, some checkpoints were established where there were members of the TO with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time the Territorial Defence operated absolutely in line with the Territorial Defence plans. The Commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence was Rade Javoric, a Serb, but he was not an SDS candidate. All the checkpoints established in the territory of the Prijedor municipality and in local communes were not points at which any checks were made. At the time these were merely sentry posts whose duty, whose responsibility, was the protection of some buildings and to look after the security of the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of weapons did you note that those sentries who were in the Muslim communities had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were old models, old Russian automatic weapons and old rifles M49, that is, made in 1949, and there were some semi-automatic rifles, M60 something. I cannot recall the model exactly. In other words, those were mostly quite old weapons that were mostly obsolete at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At some point did you become aware that weapons were being distributed to the Serbian population in the opstina on a large scale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, after this distribution of weapons, that is, when the Territorial Defence units were mobilized on a regular basis, we noticed that the number of armed members in Serb local communes was much larger than it should have been. Then on various occasions we saw how from the trucks, from military trucks, of the JNA weapons were distributed in Serb local communes after that issue. Then, by pure chance, we discovered training grounds where exercises, where drills, shooting exercises, were performed within the Kozara mountain from the village of Brezicani towards Kozara. The Serb paramilitary formations were undergoing training there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you confront Colonel Arsic with this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I received this information, I asked to see him. I warned him about those facts and he said that that was not true, and that those were some rumours which were unverified and untrue. Then I told him that we had evidence and, if he wanted to, I could show him photographs showing weapons distributed from the trucks of the Yugoslav People's Army. When I told him that, he was surprised and somewhat at a loss and then he said: "Right, we shall examine the matter".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that you also had some meetings with the Deputy Commander, Radmilo Zeljaja; what were the nature of those discussions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those meetings, I think, were held after April 6th, that is, after the commencement of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In an earlier discussion, he mentioned that he had very close ties to Sarajevo and that he had wonderful memories, reminiscences, of Sarajevo, during his army service he was in Sarajevo and that he was very fond of that city. On 6th April, Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised and I told him: "Zeljaja, listen to me. Bosnia-Herzegovina is a recognised state. It will, undoubtedly, have its own army. It would be proper for you to state your loyalty to the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to take a hand in the formation of the new army of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina". Thereupon, he expressed some doubts about the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he said: "Oh, come on, Bosnia has been recognised but nothing will come out of it". I indicated that that was not quite the case, that the European Community and the United States of America were supporting that recognition and they were backing us. I suggested that if he pledged his loyalty, we could offer him a good position in the new -- in the future army, a flat in Sarajevo and a reward, a generous pecuniary reward, if he agreed to discuss this matter. He again voiced doubts and said that hardly anything could come out of it, and I told him: "Well, if you do not want to stay here, then we can help you. If you would care to tell us what other officers in these brigades or any other individuals whom you know and who would pledge their loyalty to Bosnia-Herzegovina, we would reward you generously in money and would help you to go wherever you want". He looked very confused, very unsure of himself. He was, he seemed to waiver, very hesitant, seemed to be thinking about it, and then said: "Right, but let us not talk about this now; we can meet elsewhere." Two or three days later we met again in El Dorado which is a pub below the flat, in the building below his flat, in the building where he lived. But that other meeting did not last more than 15 minutes. We had a cup of coffee together, and he said that he was pressed for time, that he could not stay, and that there were very many activities he had to pursue. Then I tried to provoke him. I said: "What do you mean, has SDS offered you more?" and he said: "No, I am an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army and I have no contact with the SDS", and then we parted our ways and I did not have any further contacts with him after that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that you also had meetings with Simo Miskovic. What were the substance of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were quite a number of such meetings in the course of 1992, after the proclamation of the Serb municipality of Prijedor, we asked for explanations of what was behind that, what was the purpose of it, what was the Serb opstina Prijedor, and how did they think of pulling it through, how could two municipalities function in one and the same place? He used to reply: "Do not worry, it will all be easy, it will be sorted out in no time", and he never wanted to say what the true intentions were. Then there was his characteristic appearance on Radio Prijedor when the editor of Radio Prijedor, Muharem Nezirovic, invited him and me on 28th April to take part in a programme, to take together part in a radio programme. The closing sentences of his address were that he wanted us to live in peace. I am paraphrasing, of course, but the gist of his message was that SDS, that they will not be the cause of war, of a conflict, in the municipality of Prijedor. I said that neither did we have any intentions of provoking a war, a conflict, in Prijedor and we wanted peaceful life to continue, to go on, in Prijedor. Evidently, only a day later his message did not tally with their true intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What kind of meetings did you have on 29th April, the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 29th April was marked by several meetings and several events. In the early hours of the morning, I was called from Sanski Most by representatives of the SDA in Sanski Most, and asked me to come to Sanski Most and attend a meeting which would also be attended by General Talic, the then Commander of the Banja Luka corps, and Colonel Hasetic. I accepted this invitation because at the time I also acting as the President of the regional SDA board of Banja Luka which had a co-ordinating role.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What had occurred in Sanski Most that required this meeting with General Talic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as we entered Sanski Most, we were met by soldiers at a post and I told them that I was going to that meeting and they let us through. The town was swarming with army and at first I did not realise what was going on. We entered on the town hall building and General Talic and Colonel Hasetic were already there, and the Commander of the Sanski Most police representing SDA explained to me in a few words what it was all about. That evening, Serb policemen attacked non-Serb policemen, Croats, Muslims and others, and evicted them from the station, so they moved into the building of the municipal hall in Sanski Most. He said that immediately afterwards the army came down into the town. I approached General Talic and asked him for his explanation, why had the army taken control over the town? He said that it was in order to forestall conflict between, as he put it, conflicting parties and this was only temporary. I then requested that the army withdraws because he was not competent, it was not his mandate to do that, and the problem had to be solved by political means, but he refused that possibility. After that there was a meeting with Rasula, the mayor, and the President of SDA and another representative of SDA. And both the mayor and SDA President in Sanski Most urged me to attend the meeting. However, Rasula and SDS representative emphatically rejected that possibility saying that there were no representatives of Banja Luka SDS board and, therefore, refused to admit me to that meeting. After that, I left Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was your next meeting that day, on 29th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the return to Sanski -- after the return from Sanski Most, I was met in Prijedor and I was told that there would be a meeting with a policeman and other employees of the police station in Prijedor, and the meeting was to take place in the police station building. Hasan Talundzic, the chief of the police, was present at the meeting as well as several Serb superiors from the police, Muhamed Cehajic, the Mayor of the Prijedor opstina and I was at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the point of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb policemen were demanding to take a final decision whether the Prijedor police station would become part of the Banja Luka police under Stojan Zupljanin, or if it would be attached to the republic Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, as insisted upon by non-Serb policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there a resolution at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no final, definitive conclusion. I simply asked that no decision be taken at the time and to wait for the final understanding about the organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that after that understanding to be reached at the level of the Republic, final decisions should be made and that until that time the police station in Prijedor should remain as it was, that is, under the Republican Ministry of the Interior, but at the same time to maintain co-operation with the State Security centre in Banja Luka. Towards the end of the meeting, a policeman said that they did not want to follow the orders from Sarajevo. It was a Serb policeman, a policeman of Serb ethnic origin. He was the man employed in communications department, and he said that a document had just arrived saying that the police should attack the army and that he did not want that. I said that I did not know what it was all about and that was the end of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you later have a meeting with Colonel Arsic about that telegram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that meeting I went home to my flat, and some time, a little before 5 o'clock, Colonel Arsic called me by telephone and asked me to meet him in the barracks. In view of the situation as a whole, I said that it would be better to meet some other -- at some other place. He said: "Well, Simo Miskovic is already here with me, SDS President, so will you please be so kind and come too because there is an urgent matter which we have to discuss and about which I can tell you nothing over the telephone".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you go to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to the barracks and as soon as I entered the barracks he was sitting at a table and he showed me a document and said: "Do you know what this is?" I looked at it. It was a telex and I read a couple of sentences and said that I had not received any telexes from Sarajevo, and I did not know what it was all about and that that was the first time I saw anything like that. He said that this telegram was the order, that it was an order for the police and the army that the barracks of the JNA should be surrounded and all important access roads which the army could use to get out should have blockades put up. I said I knew nothing about that and that it must have been a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the course of that meeting, did it become clear or known to Colonel Arsic and the others that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had denied sending that telex and declared that it was a fake and that they had no such intentions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately after that the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina denied the contents of the document, saying that this order did not come from them and that it was a mistake. However, Arsic then turned to me and, allegedly, he said the same thing to Simo Miskovic. He said: "If either of you launches an attack against the barracks, I shall use all the means at my disposal, all the armaments I have, to fire at those who attack the army". I responded that it never occurred to us to attack the army or anyone. After that he said: "Right, in that case I suggest we go and have some dinner".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you all go and have dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. As a matter of fact, even during those previous meetings he thought, I believe, that we ought to have been happy because he had been mobilized in the Territorial Defence, and that Simo Miskovic and I should invite him and Zeljaja to a dinner. I said: "Right, all right, never mind, let us have this dinner" and he remembered that and said: "Well, now how about your keeping your promise and taking us to dinner?" and so we went to the restaurant Europa in Prijedor and, apart from my myself, there was also Hilmija Hopovac, Simo Miskovic, Zeljaja, Arsic and Zoran Karlica were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who is Zoran Karlica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did not know him at that time -- that was the first time I had seen him -- and I did not know anything about him. All I know about him is something I learnt later from other people. But then at that dinner, we stayed until 11 o'clock, and we talked at random about all sorts of things that had nothing to do with events which were underway, about general matters. I think we never even tackled a political question at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The next morning, the morning of 30th April 1992, did you receive a phone call early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on April 30th, early in the morning at 6 o'clock, I was called by Sistek Sahic, Secretary of the Municipal Committee of SDA, and he said to me: "Do you know what is new, Mirsad?" I said: "What?" "Prijedor was occupied last night". After that I went out to see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you see in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole town was swarming with military; the main communication lines leading out of town were blocked with checkpoints; all the more important buildings, Prijedor radio, the bank, the post office, the town hall, the police station, they were all under military guard and the whole picture reminded me of the films about military "putchs" that occurred in Latin America or Africa. It was like a classical coup d'etat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did it also remind you of what you had seen in Sanski Most the day before with the military check points and guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the scenario was almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there any notices posted in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were several notices. The whole of Prijedor was covered with posters and the text on these posters in Prijedor was very frequently, at every half hour or one hour, I am not sure what, read over the radio waves. The first proclamation and the poster explained why the military putch had taken place, and it was stated that SDA had usurped all power in Prijedor, that people from SDA had started to steal in enterprises, that they had started to demolish the system, that they were no better than thieves and criminals, and that the Serbian Democratic Party was forced to take this step, that the Muslim people and the other non-Serbs should have no fear about this event, that it was simply a question of removing a few criminals, whereas within six months on the outside new elections would be organised at which Muslims and Croats would have a chance to elect their new representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did these notifications indicate that the SDS was stating that it had responsibility for the takeover and was now controlling the municipal government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It was clearly stated that full control had been taken over by the SDS in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there subsequent notifications on the formation of a Krizni Stab?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the course of the same day another proclamation was issued on the Krizni Stab. It was stated that this Crisis Headquarters had been formed in Prijedor which would be in charge of all activities in Prijedor until some other changes occurred. The President of that Crisis Headquarters was Milomir Stakic, and I think that its members were Srdjo Srdic, Simo Miskovic Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they include come Colonel Arsic and Slobodan Kurusovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Slobodan Kuruzovic, I am sure that he was a member of this Stab. I am not sure whether Arsic was formerly a member. But the information I obtained later was that Slobodan Kuruzovic who took over control of the Territorial Defence and who later assumed responsibility for the entire putch in Prijedor, I learnt that he had regularly reported to Arsic on all events taking place and that it was there that he received further instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened to all of the non-Serb members of the opstina municipality government as of 30th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On April 30th, all officials, Muslims and Croats, representatives of SDA and HDZ, were removed from their posts, but not only representatives of these two parties but many other reputed citizens, Muslims and Croats, who had no connection with SDA, who were honourable and decent people, loyal citizens of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as Nedzad Seric, the President of the Court of Prijedor, Habib Bajrahtarevic, the Director of the social accounting service, SDK, for the control of payments, deputy bank director, Lika Muhamed, and many other distinguished non-Serbs holding positions that had any significance in all the institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Between the takeover on 30th April and 23rd May 1992, did you have some conversations with Srdjo Srdic about what was occurring in the opstina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that same day it was possible to hear on the Radio Prijedor waves Colonel Arsic saying that, allegedly, he had nothing to do with the described event. But I looked up Srdjo Srdic because he is a man who was most superficial among the members of the SDS, and I thought it would be easiest to learn from him what the intentions of SDS were. I telephoned him at home but his wife said he was out, and she gave me a number where I could probably find him. Judging by the telephone number, I realised that this was not within the city limits of Prijedor and that he must have been somewhere outside Prijedor because I think the number started with a "3" and Prijedor, I think, starts with a "2". I dialled this number and, indeed, Srdjo replied and I asked him: "Srdjo, what is happening? What have you done?" There was a pause and then he answered: "I and my people are ready for war, are you? Have you prepared yourself?" I answered: "For heaven's sake, Srdjo, what war? What are you talking about? Why should we go to war?" and he replied "You know very well what I am talking about and if you do not know you will learn soon enough", and he broke off. He hung up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did the SDA have meetings subsequent to this takeover to determine what action to take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On April 30th and on May 1st, I toured the whole territory of the municipality of Prijedor. On 30th April, Brdo and Ljubija, and on May 1st, Kozarac and other communities. I consulted with the local leaders and people and we came to the conclusion that an emergency meeting was necessary at which we would review the whole situation and decide what should be done, because the Serbs had actually taken over control only of the downtown part of the city and the regions in which the Serbs were a majority, whereas all the regions with a Muslim and Croat majority were under the control of Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did members of the SDA also have meetings with delegations from the SDS and the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the first meeting held between 3rd and 4th May, soon after this, therefore, we discussed what should be done next, and it was decided that it would be a good idea to send a message to the people, since Slobodan Kuruzovic at the time insisted that the Territorial Defence hand over its weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the decision to allow each municipality or each Mjesna Zajednica to make their own decision on that topic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this meeting we did not wish to take a definite decision, but we wanted to hear the voice of the people, and we instructed that rallies of citizens be convened in all the local communities and that the question should be posed at those meetings, whether the Territorial Defence should hand over their weapons or not. Our recommendation was that the weapons should not be given up. That was our recommendation, and I underline this. We did not insist on this among the citizens. The citizens accepted this recommendation, but they themselves also decided not to hand in the weapons. At the next meeting, a large meeting in the municipal council at which representatives of all the local communities were present, held two or three days later between May 6th and 7th, a current within the party insisted on negotiations with representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party and the army believing that these negotiations could achieve something. I belonged to the group of people who believed that those negotiations could achieve nothing, and that they have a clearly outlined plan of what they would do and that nothing would come of those talks, but we had nothing against those who felt that something could be achieved to go ahead and negotiate. Thus, a delegation was formed consisting, I think, of Semenovic, Mujcic, Terzic, Medunjanin, I think Islam Bahonjic as well -- I am not sure -- and they negotiated with SDS and with Arsic and Zeljaja until around May 16th when at the last meeting Zeljaja came and said: "There are no more negotiations from today on. We are the army of the Republic of Srpska. This is the Republic of Srpska. Pass on the message to your Muslims that the Territorial Defence must immediately hand over all their weapons, that all your conscripts must respond to mobilization of the Republic of Srpska and all citizens must express allegiance to the state of the Republic of Srpska." At a meeting on May 17th I was informed of this by Music and Terzic who had attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: On 23rd May was there an incident at a checkpoint in Hambarine or near Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was visiting in my parents' house and I heard some shots. I went out to see what was happening and about 300 metres in the direction of Hambarine on a bus stop, Polje, where a checkpoint of the Territorial Defence had been formed, a group of people had gathered. I went up to see what it was about and I saw a white Lada automobile -- it is Fiat, a large Italian Fiat, a luxury vehicle, a limousine -- two dead people and four wounded. I learnt that two of them were Croats, and they were lightly wounded, and they said that the four people from SDS had kidnapped them, they had forced them into the car and that they had nothing to do with them. These four, two of whom were dead and two seriously injured, bared the insignia of White Eagles and Chetnik insignia. The White Eagles are extremist formations set up by Vojislav Seselj, a Serb extremist. A member of the Territorial Defence was also injured, and he briefly tried to reconstruct the event for my benefit. They had stopped and before they managed to do anything at all, to check them out, one of them came out of the car and opened fire on members of the Territorial Defence. They lay down on the floor and at that moment one of them opened fire from an automatic rifle in the direction of the group of people I have just mentioned, and immediately after that a deserted house about one kilometre away in the field caught fire, and about 10 minutes later a military transporter appeared on the spot painted in police colours, so it appeared to be a transporter of the civilian Police Force. He insisted that Aziz Aliskovic surrender and all other members who were on that checkpoint should surrender, I told him that we cannot do that, and that it would be a good idea to form a commission to investigate the whole case. I immediately insisted that the wounded be transported to the hospital which they refused. They moved away 300 metres in the direction of Prijedor, and with a light gun, something between a gun and a machine gun, they fired at the checkpoint but there was no-one there so that nobody was hurt additionally then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Might that be a good time to take a break before we move on to something?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, would you proceed, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Dr. Mujadzic, you indicated that when you arrived at the checkpoint you were told what had occurred there by the individuals who had been wounded at the scene. Did they relate this story to you while you were attempting to treat their wounds?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just mention one matter? I do not think the witness did say he was given the account by the individuals who had been wounded. I think he was explaining that one person gave him an account. It may be my misunderstanding, but perhaps it is a matter that should be clarified as it is an important piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, I really do not recall whether the witness stated that he was told by the individuals who had actually been wounded what had happened or whether he heard from other individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I think we could scroll back through the transcript, but I do not think it is necessary to do that. I believe that is what he said but I will simply rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You can ask that question again, who told him and then we will see what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Exactly. (To the witness): Dr. Mujadzic, you have related the story of what had occurred at the checkpoint; by whom were you told what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Earlier on, I said that I talked with two of the six wounded individuals who were in the car, but that later on a TO member reconstructed the event for me; so that I draw my information both from the wounded individuals in the car and a TO member who also was wounded. So I received this information from two sides. That was what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: My following question when we began was were they describing these events to you while you were treating or attempting to treat their wounds as a physician?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I examined all the present wounded; of the six wounded, two were dead. Obviously, one had received a shot in the head and another one, I think, was hit in the head and I believe in the abdomen. He also gave no signs of life. The other two had chest wounds and did not bleed much. As a matter of fact, they did not bleed at all or, when I say they did not bleed, I mean that there was no, an open blood vessel which would bleed considerably. At that moment, while extending the first aid, the only thing I could try to do was to stop the bleeding because I had no other aids, no other implements with me. The next two were only lightly injured and their wounds presented no life hazard. Their life was not in danger -- the two in the car, I mean. A member of the Territorial Defence had his right leg injured and his right thigh, but his wounds were neither bleeding particularly profusely and his life was not in danger either, so that he was only bandaged. The thing that one had to do at that moment was to transfer all the wounded to the hospital and I insisted on that, and tried to have it done as quickly as possible because no other adequate help apart from what I did could not be extended to them on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Subsequent to this incident at the checkpoint, was there a declaration made by the Krizni Stab in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That same evening on the hills above the village of Hambarine, Rakovcani, five or six shells were fired from the decks of Prijedor, and then the next day a proclamation was broadcast on the Radio Prijedor to immediately surrender all weapons in Hambarine and surrounding villages, and that Aziz Aliskovic's group was also to surrender, it was at that checkpoint, and if they failed to do so, then the Krizni Stab would order to open fire from all available means, the settlement of Hambarine. The Krizni Stab Crisis Committee said that the villages of Hambarine should respond and thus avoid to suffer any further consequences because of a group of extremists, as they put it. Now, this document issued by the Crisis Committee was signed by Milomir Stakic, so this was the Crisis Committee order signed by Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the decision of the authorities in Hambarine with regards to turning over the weapons and the individuals from the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The local authorities decided not to turn over the weapons and men as requested by the Crisis Committee and the deadline was 12 o'clock on 24th May. As it was not done, at 12.20 the shelling of the whole hill began from artillery weapons from all directions, and it lasted until about 3 o'clock in the afternoon and then a lull took place, break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The translation of your last answer, when you said the shelling of Brdo began, was translated as "the whole hill" meaning a single hill. Were you referring to a particular hill in Hambarine being shelled or the Brdo region, as you described it earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time during the shelling I was in Aladin Sijacic's house in Celak -- in Carakovo, and the shells were falling both on Carakovo and Hambarine, and I think that Rakovcani and all the other villages in Brdo region were shelled, but I think that the principal target was the village of Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After the lull that you described at about 3 o'clock in the afternoon, what occurred next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that lull from the direction of Tukovi where that same evening to the part which was inhabited by Serbs two tanks had arrived, so two tanks moved out from there and they were followed by the infantry, and after intermittent fire which did not last long and response by the Territorial Defence on Brdo (which, I may add, had no anti-tank artillery or any mines, all they had were rifles which were issued them when Arsic was distributing those weapons), sometime around 5 or 6 o'clock p.m. those tanks climbed up the hill, that is, up the Brdo above Hambarine and took that position. One tank, later on one tank turned right and moved towards other villages and it fired at houses and buildings, aiming at everything around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Based on this attack by the infantry and the tanks, did the municipal leaders in the Brdo call a meeting which included yourself to determine whether to turn over those weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That same evening, that is, around perhaps 7.00 or 8 o'clock, very quickly almost all the weapons from the whole Brdo were collected, put on tractors and turned over, except in Carakovo and Zecovi where I was. The next day, May 25th, individuals, representatives from Carakovo and Zecovi came to me and asked me what to do. Everybody knew by that time that Biscani, Rakovcani, Hambarine, that is, the right-hand side of the Brdo region had already turned over their weapons. I told them that they should take that decision themselves, that I would not want to be the cause or influence their decision in any manner because I did not want to be responsible for anyone's life or anyone's risk because the propaganda which the SDS had launched in Prijedor, on the Radio Prijedor, and media has been trying to reduce it only so the problem within the SDA, SDA and myself, and that if people rejected me personally and SDA and other SDA leaders and they called us criminals, thieves, extremists, fundamentalists and what-not, then that everything would be all right, that nobody would lose anything. Simo Miskovic said so himself on Radio Prijedor immediately after the coup. I told those people: "Well, if you think that is better, then turn over your weapons and in that case I will go to the woods". Indeed, they did so during that day, and then with a small group of people I went to the adjacent woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the forest in the area of opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that other forests were shelled for days, I think for some twenty days that forest was shelled by Chetnik formations, and during the day on several occasions, several times, at different time intervals, and because of that we dug out a hole on a hill and spent all the time in that hole. From time to time, the brother of one of the individuals who was with me brought us some food every three or four days. We knew that there were several more groups in the forest but, because of the shelling which occurred at different time intervals, we could not move about too much. We asked that one of the individuals tried to establish contact or communication with one of those people by some roundabout way. However, he ran into Chetnik control, checkpoint. They caught him and we learned later that they tortured him, trying to find out our whereabouts. He did not tell them and they killed him with battery and the rest. After that, the elder brother came to see us in the forest because their mother knew where we were too, and for some 10 days more he also brought us food and then he told us that a special unit was being prepared, a unit to come from Nis, in order to scour the forest, that they would be bringing dogs along and all the special devices and that we could not stay there any longer, that it would be bad for our security and the security of the citizens because they would be able to conclude that they had been feeding us. We decided then to move on our way. That was on June 27th. That is about a month since the beginning of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you to locate this forest?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe first in what portion of the opstina Prijedor was the forest that you were hiding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if there is a map somewhere? I was a scout as a boy so that I know the topography. I can explain it and indicate all those sites as well as the road that we covered afterwards, all these sites that we went by and how we moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could be shown a map, I can then explain it very precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If the Exhibit could be shown to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this will be all right, yes. I think -- yes, this is fine. So this is the village of Hambarine. This is this road from Prijedor to Ljubija, and on the top of it were the units of the Chetnik formations, they climbed up there on 24th May, and cut off this part here where there are four villages, Biscani, Rizvanovici, Rakovcani and Hambarine. This is where the village, Carakovo -- if you can move it down, please -- Carakovo and the village of Zecovi. These are all the two next Muslim villages. So these four villages were immediately on 24th May turned over their weapons and Carakovo and Zecovi did it the next day. We then retreated. I was here in Carakovo and then we retreated in the forest. This is the forest which the people there called Kurevo forest. It is part of the so-called Mejdanski chain. We were here, I should say, behind the village of Brdari, near the village of Brdari. Here in the thick of the forest we dug a hole. This is where we spent all this time until June 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that you left the forest or that area after news that a special unit from Nis was being prepared to come into the forest to find you. Where is Nis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nis is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The shellings which occurred of the Brdo region on 24th, were those shellings coming from the tank and artillery positions which you indicated earlier had been set up around Prijedor from units of the 43rd and 5th Kozara Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly where each of the brigades was, what were their positions, whether it was Niska Glava or Crna Dolina, Velika Palaciste or Topica Brdo, whether it was the 43rd Brigade or the 5th Brigade. But what I am positive about is that those were the formations and the weaponry of these two brigades, but I do not know which brigade occupied which position. What is certain also is that it was from the direction of Topica Brdo, Miljakovac, Crna Dolina, from Brezicani, shells also hit Brdo. The Serb propaganda on Radio Prijedor announced, publicised posse against me and other SDA people in their propaganda. They said that in the area of this forest that there was I in person and 700, as they put it, 700 green berets, that is, 700 armed men, and that that was why the special unit from Nis had to come, which was not true at least to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned before that the 43rd was under the command of Colonel Arsic and you had had several meetings with him. Do you know where Colonel Arsic was from, his nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Arsic is a Serb by ethnic origin, but a Serb from Serbia, so he is a Serbian Serb, as we say it, a genuine Serb, and he had a specific accent and that is why I knew that he was from Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In what part of Serbia was that accent that he had, from what part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it is the central Serbian area which is called Sumadija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After you left the forest that you have described on the map on 27th June, where did you head to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there is another map showing a wider area, then I could indicate exactly the road we covered, but briefly I can say that we entered the territory of Sanski Most municipality, Stari Majdan, then we moved on to the village of Gorice, if there is a map? I do not think this map shows it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: It would be Exhibit 78, but I do not think it is necessary at this time. If you could simply describe after you -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, if this is not necessary, so I can briefly describe it, from Stari Majdan, which is in the Sanski Most municipality, moved across Fajtovac, which is also in Sanski Most opstina to Gorice, to Naskucani and Vakuf. This is all in opstina Sanski Most. From there we moved on to the Grmec Mountain. In the early hours of the morning, we passed between the villages Gornji and Donji Majkic, climbed up the Grmec Mountain and then over the mountain to the canyon of the Una River; then we climbed down the canyon and we had lots of problems and difficulties because Chetniks had noticed us. They were firing at us. Unfortunately, we lost a man there, but we did manage to swim across the Una and reach the free territory of the Bihac region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You arrived in Bihac in July of '92. What did you do while you were in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bihac, I immediately went to the hospital and began to work there as a surgeon and mostly exercised my profession there, that is, in the surgical department. In my free time, I continued my work as a Republican Member of Parliament and engaged in some other political activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Bihac and work in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Bihac, that is, we arrived in Bihac on July 13th and I stayed there until the beginning of October in 1992. Then I flew over the Serb territory in a small plane to Zagreb and then immediately proceeded to Travnik, to central Bosnia, where I stayed until the end of 1992, and there I also worked in the Travnik hospital again as a surgeon. Then I returned to Bihac by that same aircraft, the small plane -- they were such small planes which flew to Bihac -- and then the no fly decision was taken and, owing to these circumstances, I stayed in Bihac until the end of November 1993, and then I was transferred by a UN helicopter back to Travnik where I stayed until May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From there did you move on to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Travnik I also worked as a surgeon in the hospital and from there in May '94 I moved to Sarajevo where I continued to work as a surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mujadzic, you have told us that you were closely involved in the politics in the Prijedor region and became President of the SDA in Prijedor. What date did you become President of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: August 17th 1990. That was the first founding assembly when my nomination was accepted, but the real elections within the party were held next year, I think, in October '91 when I was really elected because the first time was by acclamation, but this was full elections and I was again elected President of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Before 1990 had you been involved in politics in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before 1990 I did not belong to any political organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you joined the SDA in 1990; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And at that stage the SDA was just emerging as a political party. Do you understand what I mean when I say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us at all about perhaps the numbers of members that the SDA had in Prijedor in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer this question. I cannot tell you exactly. I think there were a few thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had candidates for the elections and a number of those candidates identified themselves with your party, the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the organisation of the SDA in Prijedor presumably had a central office in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning we did not have premises because we were a newly formed organisation. So that in the private home of one of our members for a time we used his own home as temporary premises. Then after the elections we acquired premises in a building, official, real premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So was it in 1991 that the SDA started to become more organised as a political party in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the level of organisation of SDA in '91 was better than in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and when you were acclaimed President in 1990 you were President of the SDA in opstina Prijedor or just Prijedor town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have that type of organisation within the municipal board of SDA. There were 30 local organisations on a lower level than the municipal level, and there were 30 Presidents of these local committees. Each President of the local committee was an ex-officio member of the Municipal Committee, and in addition there was an Executive Board which numbered 15 members. All together the Executive Board and the President of the local committees formed the Municipal Committee as the highest body within the party which took all the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was that that you were President of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was President of both the Executive Board and the Municipal Committee because it was so proscribed by statute, that is part of the general statute of the SDA party as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So your committee of which you were President would have had districts or towns and villages in opstina Prijedor where there were local members who had a CDA representative, an SDA representative for your committee in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the expression "towns and villages" is not the most appropriate. It is better to say "smaller settlements" because on the territory of the opstina Prijedor there were, according to certain standards, the only town really was the town of Prijedor. The rest were smaller settlements and villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand what you are saying and it is these smaller villagers and settlements who also had SDA delegates of which you were the overall President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The villages and settlements who supported an SDA candidate, were they organised locally? Did they have their smaller committees within their local settlement to discuss things together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each of those 30 local committees, in each of those settlements there was a local committee which had between five and seven members. For larger settlements we agreed that the number could go up to 11 upon the request of some of the local committees, and the local committees were elected at assembly meetings of members of the local committees. Therefore, each of those settlements had their assembly consisting of members of the party living in that settlement and they elected their committee, and the President of that committee was a member of the Municipal Committee of Prijedor opstina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The number of 30 that you had as delegates for the main committee, was that because there were 30 villages or settlements or because that was a standard number that the SDA required?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number of organisations of committee members did not fully coincide with the number of settlements. I will give an example, because that was what the settlements themselves asked for. The reason was very simple. The settlements wanted to have more or less equal influence in proportion to the number of inhabitants living in this region, so that large settlements would be divided up into several local committees because our aim was that the number of members in local committees should be roughly equal. So that is how Kozarac, for instance, had 10 or 11, I cannot remember exactly, I would have to list them. Kozarac as a settlement had more than 10 local committees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying. All these committees were subject to the control, if you like, of the SDA in Prijedor; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a two-way relationship within the organisation of the party, but we did not have a firm hierarchical system; this was a rather loose system. The Presidents of local committees would come from their settlements with certain positions which would then be co-ordinated at the opstina level and where a common policy and joint decisions were taken at the level of the whole opstina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So within that organisation I suppose you had a wide variation of opinion between the different villages and settlements or the delegates that they sent as to the strategy that the SDA should adopt in dealing with the party of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, ours was a party that had a rather liberal attitude, so that within the party there was a high degree of democracy and freedom. We did not have any firm hierarchical relations of subrogation or any party constraints, and virtually all things having to do with Prijedor were decided on the basis of the positions coming from the local communities. It is also true that the range of those positions regarding certain issues was very broad, but on some other issues there was no difference of opinion regarding certain global strategic issues. All agreed, for example, that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be an integral state, that we should have good relations with the Serbs and the Croats, equally good relations with one and the other. Therefore, there was a certain spectrum of views and questions on which there was no division of views. Everybody thought it was only normal, whereas on other questions obviously there were differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you, as President of the SDA, would not insist that all the delegates spoke with the same voice; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I mentioned, as an organisation we were quite, quite liberal in our internal relationships. I must point out that we had a general platform which is contained in the SDA programme and that very rarely did we have special instructions even from our headquarters. So it would be more correct to say that initiatives and the focus of political action came from the grass root level, from the local communities rather than from members of the top leadership, me personally or somebody from the headquarters. I personally in line with the positions and setup of the party and the way people thought, my personal attitude was that all those present should express their views on all questions of any importance, and my only task in fact as the President was to try and find the best common position that would be acceptable to all, and that is how decisions were mostly taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you did not exercise much control over the grass roots of the SDA; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one might put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did membership of the SDA as you moved from 1990 to 1991 to 1992 continue to grow in the opstina Prijedor region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the majority of SDA members who joined the party did so in the period prior to the elections. After the elections the number of people joining the party was somewhat smaller, and I would say that we had a normal fluctuation; some people even dropped out and also there were others who joined. I would not say that in the course of '91 and later there was a significant increase in numbers. There was no quantitative noticeable increase in membership. Perhaps one might say that in view of the social structure later on in the course of '91 there were more members from the urban region. The number of members from the city increased in relation to the number of those from the surrounding settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I suspect like many political parties you probably had more supporters than members of the party; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I became President of the party I was never a leader. I never had any executive position. This was the first time for me to head an organisation, after all, I was only 27 then, but I understood, I grasped a rule and that is that on most questions I at least never managed to achieve greater consensus than among 60 to 70 per cent of those present. No matter how hard I tried to increase agreement on some questions to a maximum and to avoid any conflict within the party, the maximum I managed to achieve was about 60 to 70 per cent agreement on most questions. There was always 30 or 40 per cent of people who were against. I only exclude some global issues over which we all agreed, otherwise we could not be members of the party if we did not agree on some questions that were part of the party programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, but what my question was aimed at was whether in fact there were more supporters of your party than were actually signed up as members. Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you are right, there were more supporters than members of the party, but I think that too is customary in all parties. In Europe there are always more people who vote for the programme of a particular party or a party than are the number of members of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the finances of the party, the SDA in opstina Prijedor, how were you funded? Where did your money come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally drove my own car all the time. I never collected any per diems. What we consumed while working we paid for ourselves. Only at the beginning of 1992 did we get from our party headquarters a vehicle which the party headquarters purchased for us, as it did for all other Regional Committees. So a car was purchased for the Regional Committee of Banja Luka and there was the car that I was given as President of the Regional Committee and not as President of the Municipal Committee, because at the same time I held the function of President of the Regional Committee. We did not receive any other funds from our headquarters, ever. All the funds that we had were from one operation to another. When we had a large rally we would give voluntary contributions. We had the support of some of our supporters, sympathisers, private businessmen, owners of private companies who would from time to time make voluntary contributions for the benefit of the party, and that is all we had. So this was just for particular activities, otherwise it was all self-financing. We did not receive any other money from our headquarters in Sarajevo or from anywhere else, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have a subscription that was paid by the local members of the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several attempts to organise regular subscription fees in the course of 1991, and I know that certain forms came from our headquarters in Sarajevo for the collection of such subscriptions. However, that never worked properly because the idea was that all collected subscription fees should be sent to Sarajevo and then a part of those fees would be given to us. So that in some settlements some subscription fees were collected, but I think that may be only two or three settlements paid in these subscriptions on the account of the Municipal Committee. But these were symbolic sums of money and most or a part of the local committees that did collect those fees retained the money at their level, whereas most local committees did not even collect membership fees. So that we did not have a properly regulated system of subscription. I forgot to mention that, according to the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the opstina government, according to the number of representatives in the Municipal Assembly, would allot certain sums to all municipal parties. Even those sums were of a symbolic nature. So that we were very, we had very scarce resources and so we mostly financed ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have fund raising abroad? Did people contribute to the SDA funds in Prijedor who were living abroad, for instance, in Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went on a tour to Germany once only and this was upon instructions from the party headquarters, and six people collected 2,500 German marks and since they came from the region of Brdo they asked me to take that sum to the people in the region of Brdo. Since at Brdo there were six or seven local committees, I informed the people there and told them that this sum had been collected and that they should do what they wanted with it, and I gave the money to the Secretary, no, I am sorry, he was not the Secretary, he was President of one of the local committees. That was the only contribution that I had anything to do with as far as money is concerned. I remember exactly who are the people who contributed those funds originally coming from Brdo, but I do not exclude the possibility, because there were a number of settlements which behaved quite freely and we exerted no pressure on them from the Municipal Committee, so that I do not exclude there were similar such fund raising activities in the region of Kozarac, that some funds arrived from people abroad coming from Kozarac, though what I am sure of is that these were not significant sums.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not all these funds that came from abroad then passed through your hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had an account, our own legal account, and we had people working with that account and all the funds that were addressed to the Municipal Committee were deposited on that account. Just a moment please, I am saying that a symbolic amount, I will repeat, came every two or three months from the Municipal Government which was financing all parties in proportion to the number of delegates in the assembly, and from time to time there were some voluntary contributions by private entrepreneurs, but this was for a particular activity, for a concrete undertaking when we organised something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The local communes could receive money from abroad to support the SDA in their local village or settlement, and because that was not given to the municipality that did not have to go to your main account; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct.
