When anyone from a particular village or settlement, people from Kozarac, if they wanted to support a particular activity because there was quite a lot of activity, there was an idea, for instance, to renew the old tower in Kozarac dating back to the old city, there was an idea to lay an asphalt road, and there were also some activities to improve the water supply system, the telephone network, and citizens would assist such activities, but this did not go through the SDA organisation but rather through the local communes; that is the State level organisation which were like the local authorities. They were non-party, they were local authorities, whereas some other larger activities in relation to the party, I cannot remember anything of significance for which larger sums were collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have a special form that was a receipt that recorded donations to the SDA party that you signed in your own name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was a kind of receipt, a form. It is possible that there were such forms because when we received a voluntary contribution we gave out receipts. I cannot remember whether we had some special forms or perhaps they were the usual forms, but for every voluntary contribution we did give receipts to every citizen. If he gave the smaller sum he was given a receipt. Anyway, this is according to the law, this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there SDA groups in, for instance, Germany who on a local level in Germany organised collections and fund raising for your party in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the translation because I did not fully pay attention to the question in English? So could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there SDA organisations abroad, for instance in Germany, where the party was organised as the SDA of a particular town, in Germany, say Westfalen, where in that place the SDA members of that town would collect money for you, the SDA in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only in Germany but throughout Western Europe before the war associations of citizens were formed. They were not political organisations, but they were associations of citizens under the sponsorship of SDA, the Party of Democratic Action. They are not acting politically over there but only in the cultural area because the laws of the host country do not allow it. So that is one distinction. Secondly, all those organisations abroad are organisations at the level of the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For example, in Germany in Munich, in Munich there is an SDA organisation for Munich rallying members temporarily living in Munich and coming from all over Bosnia-Herzegovina, from Zvornik, Sarajevo, Prijedor, Banja Luka, all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. So abroad there is no SDA organisation for Prijedor that could collect funds just for Prijedor. Certain fund raising abroad was done but these were mostly individual, campaigns by individuals. For example, an individual would invite a friend or several friends from Prijedor or other place and say, "Let's collect some funds to help the people down there", and that is the kind of activity that was engaged in but no larger fund raising activity as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. We will stand in recess until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (1.04 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mujadzic, Hambarine and the incident that you told the court about earlier this morning ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- it was put to you that the date was 23rd May, but I think we are, in fact, talking about 22nd May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The incident at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still think that was on 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. Was your brother in the village at the same time when this incident happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in the settlement, in that settlement, where the incident happened? Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That would be Emir Mujadzic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was your cousin also there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which cousin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mehmed Avdic, was he also there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have a cousin called that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You do not have a cousin by that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In our language, a cousin is a brother's son. My brother's son is called Emir and he is four years old. Could you please specify what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In our language, a cousin would mean the son of your father or your mother's brother or sister.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: In my language, it could be both first cousin, second cousin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not really know anybody called that, Mehmed Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Avdic" spelt A-V-D-I-C?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps you mean Esad Avdic, and he is my uncle. His son is called Alan Avdic, and that is the only relative called "Avdic" that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was either your uncle or his son present at Hambarine during that day when there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which uncle, could you please specify, because I have several uncles. Do you mean the one that I mentioned, Esad Avdic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The one you mentioned, Esad Avdic, or his son also with the name Avdic, A-V-D-I-C, were either of them also present when the shooting took place in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Avdic was not there and his son Alan, I think, was 12 or 13 years old at the time, so he was a boy and he could have nothing to do with it. Esad Avdic lives about one kilometre and a half from that place and he was not even a member of the SDA or participated in any activities regarding the Territorial Defence, so that I am quite positive that he was not there and -----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it only members of the SDA who could participate in the Territorial Defence then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not hear the interpretation. I do have some technical problems. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You do not have to be a member of the SDA to be a member of the Territorial Defence, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a tendentious question. I do not know how you thought of it. I have just mentioned that Esad Avdic was neither a Territorial Defence member nor an SDA member, nor did he participate in any other activities which could be related to the event. I do not know how you establish that link, and why did you think that there was some causal relationship between the SDA and the membership in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let me make one thing clear. It is not for me to answer questions but to ask you questions. I am asking you about what took place in Hambarine when there was shooting at a roadblock. You happened to have been in Hambarine on this particular day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More specifically, it is a settlement called Polje and it is Sarajevo Street which belongs in Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could have Exhibit 79 so that we can look at where this roadblock was?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you do not have an answer yet to your question. Do you want to go back to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am taking matters, I will move on and perhaps get back to it. I am grateful to your Honour. There we have Prijedor. Can the map be moved to show Hambarine in the middle of the screen? Thank you very much, Mr. Bos. We see there Hambarine. Can you point to us as to where this roadblock was, where the shooting had occurred. That is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This here is Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you point to the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, I shall. The exact site is right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you point to where you were at the time of the shooting, if it is shown on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was somewhere here, some 3 or 400 metres towards Prijedor and that is Sarajevo Street which is part of Tukovi or, rather, this is the boundary area towards Hambarine and towards the settlement of Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long had that roadblock been in place in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, I will try to remember. Not more, I think, than some 10 to 15 days, not more than that but, at any rate, after the coup in Prijedor, that is, when the Serb Democratic Party carried out a coup in Prijedor on 29th April, it set up checkpoints at the entrances and exits from the town of Prijedor, and here there was one of these checkpoints across the bridge, on the other side of the bridge here. In this place here was the first checkpoint set up by the Territorial Defence which was set up after the coup, not less than seven days after the coup and, in any event, after April 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there other checkpoints that were situated on the roads into Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are moving away from, if you are going from Prijedor, then one checkpoint was here at the junction in Tukovi, but this was the checkpoint set up by Serb paramilitary formations, and I believe that another one was here also belonging to the Serb paramilitary formations, and the first TO checkpoint was only here almost at the entrance into Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The TO, you said, had manned that checkpoint at Hambarine where this incident took place. Would it be right to say that the members of that TO group were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were simply members of the Territorial Defence. Nobody asks a member of the Territorial Defence if he is a Muslim or not. It is a private, personal matter whether he will declare that his faith is Muslim or some other. It is the right of every individual, of every human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you will try to assist us then because I would like to know the answer, if you can give it, whether the people manning that check point, as far as you knew, were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all members were Muslims, but all inhabitants of that local commune from which TO members came are also Muslims, and there was no possibility to have any other ethnic group here, since this was a local commune, a place inhabited only by Muslims. In other places, in mixed environments, there were TO members manning those various checkpoints who were not Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Muslims who were at that checkpoint, did they have weapons with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were Territorial Defence members and they were armed, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many weapons did they have with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly. I could not say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you arrived there after the shooting and you told us that you made enquiries and you spoke to people. How many weapons did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a physician and the first thing that interested me was the state of health of the wounded, and that was my primary concern. It was a secondary matter how many weapons there were. I saw several rifles, four or five rifles, and automatic rifles, but I was also told that all four of those who were in the car of the White Eagles, members of the Chetnik paramilitary formation, that they were all armed with automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have told us you are a physician and you were concerned with the health of the people there. Forgive me for saying this, you appear to remember details about the people within the car who were Serbs or Croat, but you are unable to help with details of people outside on the checkpoint. Perhaps if you could focus your memory a little and tell us, upon reflection, as to how many weapons you saw in the possession of people who had manned the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, I will try to remember all the details. I am not sure, but I believe there were no more than four or five rifles -- it could not be more than that -- four or five rifles were in the possession of TO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who was the leader of the TO group at the checkpoint? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aziz Aliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many men did Aliskovic have with him on this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly because I did not set up those checkpoints, nor did I take part in their organisation -- it was beyond my jurisdiction -- but I think that there could not have been more than seven or eight people. As far as I can remember, I think that it could not have been more than seven or eight people. I do not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were they dressed in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were uniforms which they had been issued by the Territorial Defence of Prijedor during the legal mobilization, that is, from military depots of the Yugoslav People's Army. They were the conventional JNA uniforms in grey, olive green colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they have insignia on the uniforms to identify them in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They did not have any badge showing the lilies as insignia of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that nobody had those at this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say you attended the checkpoint after the shooting, how long did it take you to get there? What time had passed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have already said that the house that I was in was some 3 to 400 metres away, not more than that, but I do not know exactly. It took me a couple of minutes because I literally ran out of the house when I heard the shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was your brother already there or did he go to the checkpoint with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother was not there, and I do not recall that he was at that checkpoint at all. I mean, literally on that; he had come later to the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You saw him later on, you are saying, at the checkpoint rather than when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said that I never saw him. I do not remember that he ever came to that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You saw him, though, did you not, that evening in Hambarine? You saw him there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see him that evening at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you arrived at the checkpoint had you ever been to that checkpoint before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used to pass by it several times on my way to Hambarine or Ljubija, because when one goes from my parents' house where I was headed, and if one wants to go to Hambarine, Ljubija or Brdo, one needs to pass through the checkpoint and then enter Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the purpose of that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it to stop people going into Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Simultaneously with this checkpoint -- if I could be shown the map? Just a moment, I should like to show where another checkpoint was. Could I please see the map? So the checkpoint towards Hambarine, the first after Prijedor was here, and I have said that I was up here and then facing Hambarine and moving towards Hambarine, and immediately beyond Hambarine and going down here there was another checkpoint, but manned by SDS. There are some Serb houses here, and all people passed freely through this checkpoint. There were controls for security reasons only in the sense -- in view of the possible attack of Serb extremists, such as those White Eagles, these extremist Chetnik formations or some other extremist Chetnik, and I believe the fear was quite justified, as the situation in Prijedor later on demonstrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the answer is that the checkpoint was to control whoever entered the village of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. I do not think they controlled everyone, and this is not the entrance, it is simply on the way to some other places. Hambarine is a transit point, so to speak, because one has to go through Hambarine to reach some other settlements. There are up here are several other Serb villages, such as Niska Glava, Ljeskare and some more, Donji Volar is another Serb village, Niska Glava. So that citizens of Serbo-Croat origin and all the others, therefore, passed freely through this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but what is the point of putting nine men in military uniform at a checkpoint on a road with four or five rifles if it is not to control who passes that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that there was no control of those passing by. I just said that everyone was not necessarily checked, every single person who passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us look at some details then of what actually took place, you say, on 23rd May. At what time did this shooting occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the afternoon between 7.20 and 7.30 in the afternoon, evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you just visiting your parents for social reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, on 30th when the putch occurred and, as I said, I toured all the inhabited places on that day and on May 1st when I wanted to move towards Prijedor, on May 2nd I was told by some people that if I come to Prijedor the Chetnik extremists would arrest me and probably execute me. That is why from May 2nd, for reasons of safety, I had not entered Prijedor again, and all meetings that occurred after that were held in Hambarine for safety reasons. Therefore, I was in my parents' house for safety reasons because, obviously, in Prijedor I was no longer safe because the word I received was that the Serb extremists would arrest me and very probably execute me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you heard the shots you decided to see what had happened rather than leave the area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you arrived at the checkpoint what kind of car did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was an old Lada or we call it PZ, Fiat PZ127, a white old Lada.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And two people were dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that in the car itself there was no one. They were all outside the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say outside the vehicle, can you describe then where the bodies were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were right next to the car, perhaps one or two or maybe three metres from the car, one two or three. I cannot remember exactly the distance between the car and the bodies. After all, four years have gone by since.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where exactly was the car, can you tell us how it was positioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The car was right up at the checkpoint because from the moment it was stopped it did not make any more movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the car was stopped in the road at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The car had not crashed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as far as I remember, no. I cannot be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say the car was stopped at the checkpoint, was there a barrier across the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was no barrier. The car simply stopped because people from the checkpoint had stopped it by waving probably with something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The two dead bodies, where were they exactly? Can you remember where they were when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were right next to the car. I have already said, maybe one two or three metres away from the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Front or back of the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many people had travelled in the car altogether? Were you able to account for the number of people within the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Two others from the car had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where were they when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that one of them -- I cannot remember exactly, but I know that some of the wounded were standing there and they had been disarmed. They were standing next to the car. I cannot remember exactly. They were there next to the car, I think, somewhere around the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the two who had been wounded, had been disarmed, their weapons taken away from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four were Serbs wearing uniforms with insignia of White Eagles, the insignia of the extremist Seselj Chetnik organisation, and I think that two of them who were driving the car were of Croatian nationality, and I think they were in civilian clothes, and they told me that they had nothing to do with this and that these four men had forced them to drive that car, to take the men and to drive them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The two who were dead were also Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two who were dead were Serbs but the two Croats were also wounded. All six of them were hit because, as far as I was told by those present, one of the TO members fired without actually taking aim and he hit all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: With one shot he hit all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, with a machine gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A burst of fire, automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- without taking aim he managed to kill two and wound two others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were six people in the car and he fired in their direction. Two out of those six died and the other four were wounded, two more seriously and two less seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So everyone who had been in the car had injuries caused by shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The result of the injuries to the TO checkpoint was one person injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one TO member was injured, wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What happened to the wounded people? You say that they were two Croats and two Serbs. What happened to them? Where did they go after you had arrived at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As telephone lines were totally cut with the town of Prijedor, it was not possible to ask for an ambulance to come to pick up the wounded. There was a special system -- I am not very well versed in technical equipment-- some kind of mini radio system, so that it was possible, somebody proposed that using this system we could report to the centre in Prijedor for information; and I immediately to Rizvanovici to try and call the information centre and let them know what had happened, and to ask somebody from the hospital, the emergency service, to come immediately and care for the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were the four people who were wounded who had been in the car taken to hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I cannot say because, as I said, immediately after this event the police car, the armoured transporter, that immediately arrived on the spot, and which I asked to take in these people and they refused, they moved away 300 to 400 metres, maybe more, 500 or 600, I cannot say exactly, and they fired at the checkpoint. After that, it was already dusk, and tanks arrived in Tukovi and certain units. Everything was blocked in Tukovi along the next kilometre towards Prijedor with military formations of the SDS. After trying to report to Prijedor what had happened, I learnt later that someone afterwards came from Prijedor with a car and drove those people away -- at least that is what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us look at when the police vehicle arrives after the shooting, and asks that the leader of the TO group, Aliskovic, should surrender.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see the people speaking from the transporter. They did not even come out of the transporter. They spoke through the opening, issuing orders and they demanded that Aziz and all the other people should surrender. I just told them that a commission should be formed to investigate the case rather than arresting people just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What do you mean "arresting people just like that"? There were two people dead, four people injured and the police had arrived. Why should you say that there should be a commission to investigate what had happened? The people of the TO at that roadblock had done the shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but you forget that this was no lawful police, that these were ordinary criminal elements, and that the legal Chief of Police had been dismissed by the coup.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You wanted a commission to investigate it to avoid those people of the TO at the roadblock being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who should arrest whom because, if we viewed things from the legal aspect, then the people who came with the police should have been arrested, because they were the ones who had caused the incident and had overthrown the legal state system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not think, as the President of a political party in the area with a responsibility, that where killings had taken place in that way there should be investigation by the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, but by legal bodies, legal police forces and these people who came there were not that; and I was responding as a deputy and member of the Republican Parliament of the Council of Citizens, the highest legislative body of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not know who those policemen were that were in that vehicle, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I knew for sure was that they were not representatives of the legal authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Anyway, they did not show any documents, they did not even come out of the vehicle but, by the insignia on the vehicle, it was clear that these were extremist SDS forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is what you say, but you were quite happy for this shooting and these killings to take place and for any due process of law to be avoided, were you not, Mr. Mujadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that your question is tendentious. I do not know how you concluded that I wanted that shooting to take place because I happened to hear about it quite by chance. That is my first point and, secondly, it is quite certain that the people from the car were the first to fire at TO members without any warning, and that the response of one of the TO members was in self-defence, as he was falling to the ground while the people were shooting at them from the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How on earth can you say that when you were not there, you did not see who fired the first shots, you come to the scene and there are two Serbs dead, four others from the car wounded, and you say they are extremists who started it, and you have one person slightly injured from the TO; you have been impartial about this, have you not, Mr. Mujadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I described the whole case absolutely impartially because you forget that two out of these six people were Croats who had nothing to do with the four Serb extremists, members of the White Eagles, the most extremist Chetnik organisation, who confirmed that that is how it happened; and, anyway, one of those present, Serbs, also confirmed this and all the other eyewitnesses who saw this event, that without any warning one of the members of the White Eagles had started shooting at TO members, so I do not see why I am partial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Additional questions, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, beginning on 27th June when you were hiding in that hole in the woods for a month being shelled on a daily basis, did any of these police authorities attempt to intervene and assist your group?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, I am not sure how that follows from cross-examination as a matter arising, or whether it is an opportunity for a speech from my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If that is an objection ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- I will overrule the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a price on my head and Stojan Zupljanin personally declared that negotiations in Bihac in the presence of Zijed Kadic that they would catch me at all cost and that there was no way I could escape. The Serb propaganda reported on a daily basis whether I had been captured and whether anyone had seen me and, according to information I received, a price was offered to anybody who would report about my whereabouts or who would capture me. Finally, when they did not manage to find me and capture me, they published that they had torn me asunder between two vehicles and then Abdulah Konjici, President of the Council of Citizens, addressed a letter of protest because of such a brutal act and, indeed, all people in Sarajevo believed that that was what had happened. However, thank God, that was just Serb/Chetnik propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Additional questions, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have, I think, three questions to ask you. The first question relates to the incident that you described when the tanks arrived and there was, you say, concern on the part of citizens as to what the meaning of this event was. Can you tell me, was that at a time when fighting was going on in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that by then the war in Croatia had started, had got well underway, and the media in Zagreb and Belgrade presented the war in Croatia in totally different ways. From the Zagreb media, we learned of terrible crimes and bloodshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I am only concerned with the question whether when the tanks arrived that was a time when there was fighting in Croatia and I think you have answered that "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Then the second question I wanted to ask you was about Dr. Karadzic's position when he made the statement in the Republic's Assembly that horrified delegates. What was the position he was then holding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was then President of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And, accordingly, a member of the Assembly, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the permission of the parliament, someone who is not a member of the parliament may speak, so that Karadzic was speaking only in the capacity of President of the Party. He was not a member of parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. The third question is this reference to "lilies". I have read in a number of exhibits that some forces wore lilies as a badge and you were asked about lilies in cross-examination. Can you tell us something about this badge and who wore it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was still early on and those badges were worn by some TO members who, by chance, managed to find or draw that sign; not all members of TO because there were very few such signs around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Subsequently, did it become a recognised badge of any particular force in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but if you are thinking of the very beginning whether there was any other organisation which had that sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: But later then it became the official insignia of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Mujadzic, when you took refuge in the forest were you and your companions armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with personal arms. I had a pistol that was normally registered, a Magnum 357 -- I had a permit a licence for it -- and the people who were with me also had pistols.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, you indicated on April 30th -- I believe that was the date -- that military came into Prijedor. What military was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are probably thinking of the forces that carried out the putch and which I saw early on April 30th in front of the most important buildings, at the entrances of places. Those were forces of the 5th Kozara Brigade, paramilitary formations of the Serbian Democratic Party. Then there were also some special forces, special units, from Banja Luka, and Banja Luka special police forces and some people of whom I do not know which units they belong to, they were from Klujc, Dubica, from other municipalities outside Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The 5th Kozara Brigade, is that from Serbia, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from Croatia, or was it part of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 5th Kozara Brigade is a brigade of which Colic Pero was in command and which had fought in Croatia on the front of Lipik and Pakrac and which, together with the 43rd Brigade, returned to Prijedor. It was part of the Banja Luka corps brigade, belonging to the Banja Luka corps of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that Colonel Arsic was a Serbian from Serbia. What army was he in, a Colonel of what military unit, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Have you any objection to Dr. Mujadzic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. You may be permanently excused. Thank you, Dr. Mujadzic, for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, will you call your next witness, Mr. Tieger, or both of you -- Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The next witness will testify in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then we will go into closed session.

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing in closed session–released by Trial Chamber II on 13 October 1996)
